comparison: Both strongly support that adolescents performed worse on hard discrimination tasks (C2, C29-C31, C48). OpenEval includes C3 (behavioral mechanisms) which peer review addresses separately in R2. Both evaluations cite the same statistical evidence from Figures 1i-j and 3g.

Perfect agreement on claims C26, C27, C45, C47 regarding equivalent learning on procedural and easy discrimination tasks. Both evaluations support that age differences manifest only on hard tasks, with peer review implicitly accepting this by focusing discussion on hard task differences.

Both strongly support the cognitive control interpretation (C36-C41). OpenEval includes C50 (lick bias in head-fixed paradigm) while peer review focuses on the perceptual sensitivity vs. cognitive control dissociation (C37-C38). Both describe this analysis as particularly compelling.

Perfect agreement on claims C43, C55 regarding greater performance instability in adolescents. Both evaluations support the coefficient of variation analysis, with peer review implicitly accepting this as part of the 'well designed' behavioral characterization.

Both support neural discrimination findings (C61-C63) with OpenEval providing more comprehensive coverage including C74-C78 (AUC analysis details). Peer review emphasizes single-cell and population-level discrimination (C65, C67-C68), describing the neuronal recording approach as 'particularly powerful.'

Partial overlap on learning-related claims. OpenEval R5 addresses C74-C78 (AUC analysis) while peer R4 focuses on C4, C9, C79-C80 (age-learning interactions). Both support that neural differences reflect both age and learning effects.

Partial overlap on population-level neural findings. OpenEval R6 covers linear discriminant analysis (C64-C69) while peer R3 includes some overlapping claims (C65, C67-C68) as part of broader neural discrimination findings. Both support task-difficulty-specific effects.

Both address age-learning interactions (C4, C9, C79-C80) with OpenEval also including correlation analyses (C81-C82). Peer review describes the novice-expert comparison as 'completing the research question in a convincing way.'

Partial overlap on correlation between neural and behavioral measures (C81-C82). OpenEval R7 covers broader learning effects while peer R10 specifically addresses the neural-behavioral correlation, both supporting the relationship.

Perfect agreement on claims C83-C87 regarding learning-induced plasticity in frequency tuning. Both support that adults show stronger plasticity than adolescents, with peer review confirming 'neuronal tuning properties had changed in adults but not in adolescent.'

Perfect agreement on optogenetic findings (C52-C54). However, OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to potential confounds (arousal, motivation), while peer review rates as SUPPORTED, describing optogenetic experiments as 'completing the research question in a convincing way.' This represents a notable difference in interpretation.

Perfect agreement on claims C28, C46 regarding cognitive interference when task demands increase. Both evaluations support this finding across both behavioral paradigms, with peer review implicitly accepting as part of the 'well designed' behavioral task.

OpenEval addresses C32 (sequential training necessity) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. OpenEval notes this establishes methodological constraints without revealing age-specific differences.

Perfect agreement on claims C33-C34, C44 regarding trial count analyses ruling out trial number as a confound. Both evaluations support that performance differences are not due to motivation or engagement differences.
OpenEval addresses C35 (linear mixed effects controlling for sex and housing) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. This methodological control is supported by Table 1 analysis.

OpenEval addresses C42, C51, C56-C57 (inter-trial interval and lick behavior) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. These findings complement lick bias results and characterize immature cognitive control.

OpenEval addresses C70-C71 (variance analysis showing similar effects of task difficulty on neural variability) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. Age differences manifest in separation rather than dispersion.
OpenEval addresses C73 (novice recordings captured pre-learning responses) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. This confirms the experimental design for learning comparisons.

Both address speculative mechanistic claims (C88, C91) about feedback pathways. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of direct experimental evidence, while peer review rates as SUPPORTED without challenging the speculation. This represents different standards for evaluating interpretative claims.
OpenEval addresses C1, C10-C22 (background knowledge and literature review) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. These provide context but are not novel findings.

OpenEval addresses C92-C93 (primary conclusions synthesizing major findings) with no corresponding peer review evaluation. These represent the study's main conclusions about developmental differences in auditory discrimination.

Peer review R3 includes claims C6, C7, C8 (additional neural discrimination details) not explicitly grouped in any OpenEval result. These are part of the broader neural findings that OpenEval distributes across R5 and R6.
